title: Beals Street to the Eternal Flame: PT-109, the Thirteen Days, and the Order About Silver
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Brookline, 83 Beals Street: the second son
stops.date_confidence: attested. Corrected pin: the research pool gave 42.3373, -71.1219, about 1.1 km south of the house; the John F. Kennedy National Historic Site at 83 Beals Street is at 42.3469, -71.1233.
stops.campa: In a wood-frame house on Beals Street in Brookline a second son is born to Joseph P. Kennedy and Rose Fitzgerald, daughter of a mayor of Boston. They name him John Fitzgerald. Nine children will pass through this house and the larger ones that follow it, and the family's ambition is already assigned elsewhere: the eldest son, Joseph Jr., is the one being raised for office. The second son is the sick one, in and out of bed with fevers and stomach trouble, reading in an upstairs room of a house his mother will one day furnish again from memory for the government to keep.
suggested_refs: The John F. Kennedy National Historic Site, 83 Beals Street, Brookline, restored by Rose Kennedy from memory
sources: National Park Service, John F. Kennedy National Historic Site

stops.name: New Milford, Canterbury School: the year cut short
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month (September 1930). Corrected pin: the pool gave 41.6702, -73.4133, about 9 km north of the school and outside New Milford; Canterbury School, 101 Aspetuck Ave, is at 41.5864, -73.4126.
stops.campa: At thirteen he is sent to Canterbury above the Housatonic, the first time he lives away from home and the only Catholic school he will ever attend. He does badly at Latin and well at English and writes home about football and about being hungry. Illness closes the year before it ends and he does not go back; the sources reachable here say only that sickness cut the stay short, and do not name it. He is entered at Choate the following autumn without discussion. Illness will end two more enrolments before he turns nineteen.
suggested_refs: Canterbury School records for the 1930-31 year, the only Catholic schooling of his life

stops.name: Wallingford, Choate: the Muckers
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month for entry (September 1931); graduation June 1935.
stops.campa: Four years at Choate, from September 1931, are spent in the shadow of Joseph Jr., who is head prefect and football captain and everything the school rewards. The younger brother answers by founding the Muckers, a club organized around insubordination whose members the headmaster comes close to expelling. He charms every adult in the place and impresses almost none of them academically. He graduates in June 1935, sixty-fourth in a class of one hundred and twelve.
suggested_refs: Choate yearbook and headmaster's correspondence on the Muckers Club, 1934-35

stops.name: London, the London School of Economics: a fortnight of illness
stops.date_confidence: attested: sailed 25 September 1935. Sequence corrected against the pool, which placed this after Princeton and framed it as recovery. LSE came first, and the jaundice ended it (LSE History, 'The almost alumnus').
stops.campa: He sails from New York in September 1935 to read at the London School of Economics under Harold Laski, the Marxist theorist his father has decided the boy should hear argue in person. He registers and hardly attends. Within a week he is in hospital with jaundice, and about three weeks after landing he sails home again. The American education that follows is the second choice, not the first. The whole of his direct schooling in Marxism fits inside that one month, and most of it is spent in a hospital bed.
suggested_refs: LSE registration records for Michaelmas 1935 under Harold Laski
sources: LSE History, 'The almost alumnus: John Fitzgerald Kennedy'

stops.name: Princeton, six weeks and the jaundice again
stops.date_confidence: attested: matriculated 26 October 1935, six weeks into the academic year, after the abandoned London term.
stops.campa: Home from London, he matriculates at Princeton on the twenty-sixth of October, six weeks into a year already formed, following his friend Lem Billings into a class that has stopped needing new members. Jaundice returns before Christmas and he withdraws after roughly two months. He spends the winter recovering, and enters Harvard the following autumn, where his brother already is. Two universities have been begun and abandoned inside a single calendar year, both of them on the body's terms.
suggested_refs: Princeton registrar's record of the abandoned autumn term, 1935

stops.name: Cambridge, Harvard College: the thesis that becomes a book
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month for entry (September 1936); degree 1940.
stops.campa: He enters Harvard College in the autumn of 1936 and is an undistinguished student for two years, spending his long vacations in Europe while his father sits as ambassador in London. The senior thesis he writes on British appeasement and rearmament earns him a cum laude degree in government in 1940 and is published the same year as a book, Why England Slept. In the autumn he audits business courses at Stanford for a term, leaves for South America, and never enters a classroom again. The war is two years old in Europe and one year away from him.
suggested_refs: The Harvard senior thesis of 1940, published as Why England Slept

stops.name: London, Prince's Gate: the ambassador's house
stops.date_confidence: attested to the period 1938-1939; the pool gives no exact date for the residence, so the month defaults to September 1938.
stops.campa: Joseph Kennedy is Roosevelt's ambassador to the Court of St James's, and the family takes the embassy residence at Prince's Gate across from Hyde Park. From this address the second son travels the continent through 1938 and 1939, watching the descent to war at the height of his father's campaign to keep America out of it. What he sees becomes the argument of the Harvard thesis: not that appeasement was wicked, but that a democracy arms itself slowly and had better know that about itself in time. The ambassador's politics will not survive the war. The son's book will.
suggested_refs: The US Embassy residence at 14 Prince's Gate, London, 1938-1940

stops.name: Blackett Strait, the Amagiri out of the dark
stops.date_confidence: attested. Corrected pin: the pool gave -8.1167, 157.2, about 22 km too far east, on or near Kolombangara rather than in the strait; Blackett Strait is centred at -8.1167, 157.000.
stops.campa: He has trained on Narragansett Bay at Melville and taken command of the patrol torpedo boat PT-109 at Tulagi on the twenty-fourth of April. Just after two in the morning of the second of August, running dark in Blackett Strait with the engines throttled down, the Japanese destroyer Amagiri comes out of the night at speed and cuts the boat in half. Two of the thirteen aboard are killed at once. The bow floats; fuel burns on the water around it; and eleven men hold to the wreck until the afternoon, when it begins to settle under them.
suggested_refs: The US Navy action report on the loss of PT-109, Blackett Strait, 2 August 1943

stops.name: Plum Pudding Island, the strap in his teeth
stops.date_confidence: attested. Corrected pin: the pool gave -8.0578, 156.9469, about 7.5 km off; Kennedy Island (Plum Pudding, Kasolo) is at -8.1128, 156.9056.
stops.campa: With the hull going under they swim for a scrap of land chosen because it is too small to be garrisoned. Kennedy takes the strap of the burned engineer Patrick McMahon's life jacket in his teeth and tows him the whole way, four hours in the water, McMahon unable to swim. The islet is Kasolo, which the Americans call Plum Pudding: a hundred yards of coconut palm, no fresh water. Every man who went into the water comes out of it. The place will be renamed Kennedy Island, and the tow, told and retold, will run in every campaign he ever enters.
suggested_refs: Kennedy Island (Kasolo), Solomon Islands, renamed for the swim of 2 August 1943

stops.name: Olasana Island, Biuku Gasa and Eroni Kumana
stops.date_confidence: the pool attests only the month, 1943-08; the day here follows the standard rescue chronology and is reconstruction. Corrected pin: the pool gave -8.0644, 156.955, about 7.5 km off; Olasana is at -8.1320, 156.9087.
stops.campa: There is nothing to drink on Plum Pudding. After two days he moves the crew again, swimming and towing McMahon a second time, to Olasana, which is larger and carries coconuts and better cover. Here two Solomon Islander scouts working for the Allied coastwatchers, Biuku Gasa and Eroni Kumana, paddle in and find eleven Americans on a beach that is supposed to be empty. The rescue that follows belongs to them and to the network behind them. For fifty years the American telling of the story will keep their names small, or leave them out of it altogether.
suggested_refs: Biuku Gasa and Eroni Kumana, coastwatcher scouts, Olasana Island, August 1943

stops.name: Naru Island, the message cut into a coconut
stops.date_confidence: the pool attests only the month, 1943-08; the day here follows the standard rescue chronology and is reconstruction. Corrected pin: the pool gave -8.0489, 157.1, about 20 km off in open water; Naru is at -8.1388, 156.9173, roughly 1.2 km from Olasana.
stops.campa: He swims across to Naru, a bit over a kilometre from Olasana, looking for anything the Japanese have left behind and for a way to signal out. There is no paper on the island. He cuts the message into the husk of a green coconut instead: where they are, how many are alive, come and get them. Gasa and Kumana carry the coconut by canoe through patrolled water to the coastwatchers, and it is that shell, not any radio, that gets the crew of PT-109 off the reef. Twenty years later it will sit on his desk in the Oval Office, set in wood and plastic.
suggested_refs: The PT-109 coconut shell, later a paperweight on the Oval Office desk

stops.name: Hyannis Port, the brother killed over England
stops.date_confidence: the death is attested to 12 August 1944 over England; the pin is the Kennedy compound, where the family was, and is reconstruction, the pool giving no coordinates for either the death or the receipt of the news. Corrected compound pin: the pool gave 41.6362, -70.2802, about 1.9 km east in Hyannis harbour; the compound is at 41.6300, -70.3024.
stops.campa: In November he takes command of PT-59 and runs a rescue of trapped marines; on the eighteenth he is relieved of PT-boat command, his back and his health finished with small boats, and he is awarded the Navy and Marine Corps Medal for Blackett Strait. He retires from the Naval Reserve in March 1945. Between those dates, on the twelfth of August 1944, Joseph Jr., the son the family has been building for the presidency since the day he was born, is killed when his explosives-laden bomber detonates over England on a volunteer mission. The ambition transfers within the year.
suggested_refs: The Kennedy compound at Hyannis Port, where the news of Joseph Jr.'s death reached the family

stops.name: East Boston, the eleventh district
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month (November 1946); the pool gives the year for the election and 3 January 1947 for the seat.
stops.campa: He runs for the eleventh congressional district of Massachusetts, the working-class seat of East Boston and Charlestown and the North End, at twenty-nine, with a war hero's press, his father's money, and a household of brothers and sisters working the wards. He wins going away. The candidate the district elects is thin, often in pain, and privately unsure he wants the job at all, since it was assigned to him by his brother's death rather than chosen. He will hold the seat for three terms and leave almost no legislative trace on it.
suggested_refs: The 1946 Democratic primary in Massachusetts's 11th district, his first campaign

stops.name: The Capitol, three terms in the House
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He takes his seat on the third of January 1947 and serves six years as a backbencher, a tenure interrupted repeatedly by illness and by a back that will not hold him upright through a working week. He votes with labour on housing and against his party on other things and is bored by most of it. The career is not being decided in this building. It is being decided in Massachusetts, county by county, in four years of methodical touring and small halls that nobody in Washington is bothering to watch.
suggested_refs: The Eightieth Congress, in which he sat as a freshman member alongside Richard Nixon

stops.name: Boston, the seat taken from Lodge
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month (November 1952); seat taken 3 January 1953.
stops.campa: In November 1952 he takes the Senate seat from the incumbent Henry Cabot Lodge Jr., in a year the Republican presidential ticket carries Massachusetts comfortably. The campaign is run out of Boston headquarters and organized largely by his brother Robert, in his first work of this kind: house parties, ward captains, a card index of the whole state. He takes his seat on the third of January 1953. He is thirty-five years old and has been in elective office for six of them.
suggested_refs: The 1952 Massachusetts Senate campaign, Robert Kennedy's first management

stops.name: Newport, St Mary's Church: the wedding
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He marries Jacqueline Lee Bouvier at St Mary's Roman Catholic Church in Newport on the twelfth of September 1953, the reception following at Hammersmith Farm, her stepfather's estate above Narragansett Bay. Crowds break the police lines outside the church to see them come out. He is thirty-six and a first-term senator; she is twenty-four; and the wedding is covered by the national press as though he already held the office he intends to hold. The marriage is photographed from this morning onward without a break.
suggested_refs: St Mary's, Newport, and Hammersmith Farm, 12 September 1953
sources: JFK Library, 'Wedding of Jacqueline Bouvier and John F. Kennedy'

stops.name: New York City, the spine and the book
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month (October 1954, Hospital for Special Surgery). The pin is a generic New York City coordinate: the pool gives the city only, with no hospital coordinates. This is the weakest pin in the file.
stops.campa: In October 1954 he is taken to New York for spinal fusion, the back injured at Harvard and finished off in the Pacific having put him on crutches. He nearly dies of infection, is given last rites, and undergoes a third operation in February 1955. Out of the long convalescence comes Profiles in Courage, studies of senators who broke with their parties, published in January 1956 and awarded the Pulitzer Prize for Biography in 1957. His aide Ted Sorensen states in 2008 that he wrote first drafts of most of the chapters. In November 1957 his daughter Caroline is born.
suggested_refs: Profiles in Courage (January 1956) and the 1957 Pulitzer Prize for Biography
sources: JFK Library timeline and 'About the Book'
Straight Dope, 'Did John F. Kennedy really write Profiles in Courage?'

stops.name: Los Angeles, the nomination on the first ballot
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He wins the Democratic nomination on the first ballot at Los Angeles on the thirteenth of July, having taken the primaries state by state against the objection that no Catholic can be elected. He offers the second place on the ticket to Lyndon Johnson, the Senate majority leader who fought him for the nomination and who despises him, and Johnson takes it. Two days later, in the open air at the Coliseum, he accepts, and gives the campaign the name it will be filed under: the New Frontier.
suggested_refs: The 'New Frontier' acceptance speech, Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum, 15 July 1960

stops.name: Chicago, WBBM: the first televised debate
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the twenty-sixth of September, from a Chicago studio, he meets Richard Nixon in the first televised debate between American presidential candidates. Nixon arrives ill and underweight and refuses makeup. Kennedy addresses the camera rather than his opponent and looks like the healthier of the two men, which he is not. Theodore White, watching, dates the reshaping of the race to this hour, and what he writes about afterward is not the policy but the two faces.
suggested_refs: Theodore White, The Making of the President 1960, on the first debate
sources: Theodore White, The Making of the President 1960

stops.name: Hyannis Port, election night
stops.date_confidence: attested. Corrected compound pin as above: 41.6300, -70.3024, not the pool's 41.6362, -70.2802.
stops.campa: The family gathers at the Cape Cod compound to watch the returns, the houses wired with telephones and teletype for the night. It is one of the closest elections ever held in the country and it is not settled until the morning. He is forty-three, the youngest man ever elected to the office and the first Catholic to hold it. Seventeen days later his son John Jr. is born in Washington. The transition is run out of the compound, in the same rooms and by the same brothers and sisters who ran the campaign.
suggested_refs: The Kennedy compound on election night, 8 November 1960

stops.name: The Capitol, the inauguration in the cold
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He takes the oath at noon on the twentieth of January, on the East Portico of the Capitol, in bitter cold after a snowstorm, bareheaded and without an overcoat. He is the youngest man elected to the office and the first Catholic in it. The inaugural address says almost nothing about the country's domestic business; it is addressed outward, to allies, to adversaries, and to the new nations, and it closes with a charge to the citizens standing in front of him that will be quoted back at his successors for the rest of the century.
stops.quote: Ask not what your country can do for you, ask what you can do for your country.
stops.quote_source: John F. Kennedy, Inaugural Address, Washington D.C., 20 January 1961 (transcript, The American Presidency Project / JFK Library)
suggested_refs: The inaugural address of 20 January 1961, delivered from the East Portico

stops.name: The White House, the Bay of Pigs
stops.date_confidence: attested. Canonical White House pin inherited byte-identical from the Lincoln file (38.8977, -77.0365).
stops.campa: Three months into the term, a brigade of Cuban exiles trained and armed by the CIA under a plan inherited from Eisenhower lands at the Bay of Pigs. Fidel Castro directs the defence in person; the air cover the exiles were promised is withheld; in three days it is over, with about twelve hundred prisoners taken who will later be ransomed for baby food and medicine. Kennedy takes public responsibility at a news conference four days after the landing and privately stops believing the agency that told him it would work. The failure buys him the argument he will use eighteen months later.
stops.quote: There's an old saying that victory has 100 fathers and defeat is an orphan.
stops.quote_source: John F. Kennedy, News Conference 10, 21 April 1961 (transcript, The American Presidency Project), four days after the landing
suggested_refs: JFK Library, 'The Bay of Pigs'; the Brigade 2506 prisoner ransom of December 1962

stops.name: Vienna, the summit with Khrushchev
stops.date_confidence: attested to 3-4 June 1961; the pool's chronology gives only the month.
stops.campa: After Paris, where a state dinner is given for them at Versailles and his wife's French carries the visit, he meets Nikita Khrushchev over two days in Vienna. Khrushchev, reading the Bay of Pigs as weakness, spends the summit lecturing and threatening Berlin. Kennedy comes out of it shaken and calls it afterward the roughest thing in his life. Two months later the Wall goes up across Berlin. The two men never meet again: everything between them from here runs through letters, through back channels, and once, for thirteen days, in public.
suggested_refs: Frederick Kempe, Berlin 1961, on the Vienna summit and its consequences

stops.name: Houston, Rice Stadium: the moon
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: In September heat at Rice Stadium he commits the country to putting a man on the moon before the decade is out and returning him alive, a programme with no existing hardware and no proven method for any stage of it. The speech makes an argument out of difficulty as such: the reason for going is that it is hard. He will not see any of it. The launch complex on the Florida coast will be renamed for him within days of his death, and it is there, in 1986, that Richard Feynman will drop a piece of O-ring rubber into a glass of ice water and explain what went wrong.
stops.quote: We choose to go to the Moon in this decade and do the other things, not because they are easy, but because they are hard.
stops.quote_source: John F. Kennedy, Address at Rice University, Houston, 12 September 1962 (transcript, JFK Library archives)
suggested_refs: The Rice University address of 12 September 1962; Launch Complex 39, Kennedy Space Center

stops.name: The White House, the quarantine announced
stops.date_confidence: attested. Canonical White House pin inherited byte-identical from the Lincoln file.
stops.campa: On the sixteenth of October he is shown U-2 photographs of Soviet medium-range missile sites under construction in Cuba. For six days the discovery is held inside the executive committee while the options are argued out: strike, invade, blockade. On the twenty-second he goes on television and tells the country what is on the island and that the Navy will quarantine it, and that any missile fired from Cuba at any nation in this hemisphere will be treated as an attack by the Soviet Union upon the United States. Fidel Castro, whom Moscow did not consult, hears the American terms as the rest of the world hears them.
stops.quote: This Government, as promised, has maintained the closest surveillance of the Soviet military buildup on the island of Cuba.
stops.quote_source: John F. Kennedy, Radio and Television Address to the Nation on the Soviet Arms Buildup in Cuba, 22 October 1962 (transcript, JFK Library)
suggested_refs: The U-2 photographs of 14-16 October 1962 and the ExComm tapes
sources: U.S. State Department Office of the Historian, 'The Cuban Missile Crisis, October 1962'

stops.name: The White House, the letters of the twenty-seventh
stops.date_confidence: attested. Canonical White House pin inherited byte-identical from the Lincoln file.
stops.campa: On the twenty-sixth Khrushchev writes privately, offering removal in exchange for a pledge not to invade, and warning that the two of them should not pull on the ends of the rope in which the knot of war is tied. On the twenty-seventh a second and harder letter demands the Jupiter missiles out of Turkey, and an American U-2 is shot down over Cuba. Kennedy answers the first letter and ignores the second in public, while Robert Kennedy tells the Soviet ambassador privately that the Turkish missiles will go. On the twenty-eighth Moscow announces withdrawal. Castro, consulted about neither the missiles nor their removal, hears it on the radio.
stops.quote: The first thing that needs to be done, however, is for work to cease on offensive missile bases in Cuba and for all weapons systems in Cuba capable of offensive use to be rendered inoperable, under effective United Nations arrangements.
stops.quote_source: Letter, John F. Kennedy to Nikita Khrushchev, 27 October 1962 (text at atomicarchive.com / State Department FRUS 1961-63 vol. VI)
suggested_refs: Khrushchev's letter of 26 October 1962, facsimile at the JFK Library Cuban Missile Crisis microsite
sources: U.S. State Department Office of the Historian

stops.name: The White House, Executive Order 11110
stops.date_confidence: attested. The pool said Congress 'passed' Public Law 88-36 on this date; Congress passed the bill in April and May 1963 and Kennedy signed it on 4 June, the same day he signed the order. Canonical White House pin inherited byte-identical from the Lincoln file.
stops.campa: On the fourth of June he signs the repeal of the Silver Purchase Act of 1934, ending the Treasury's obligation to buy silver against certificates, and the same day signs Executive Order 11110, amending an order of Truman's so that the Treasury Secretary may issue silver certificates and coin silver dollars through the phase-out. The travel is toward Federal Reserve notes and away from silver; his own economic report says that except in coins, silver serves no useful monetary function. Andrew Jackson killed a central bank. Abraham Lincoln printed greenbacks around one. This order does neither, and will be read for sixty years as though it did.
stops.quote: The authority vested in the President ... to issue silver certificates against any silver bullion, silver, or standard silver dollars in the Treasury not then held for redemption of any outstanding silver certificates, to prescribe the denominations of such silver certificates, and to coin standard silver dollars and subsidiary silver currency for their redemption.
stops.quote_source: Executive Order 11110, signed by John F. Kennedy, 4 June 1963 (text, The American Presidency Project)
suggested_refs: Executive Order 11110 and Public Law 88-36, both signed 4 June 1963; silver redemption ends 24 June 1968
sources: The American Presidency Project, text of EO 11110

stops.name: American University, the strategy of peace
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Six days after the silver order he gives the commencement address at American University and asks the country to reexamine its own attitude toward the Soviet Union and toward the Cold War as such, on the ground that both sides are caught in a cycle in which suspicion on one side breeds suspicion on the other. The speech is delivered weeks before the Partial Test Ban negotiations advance in Moscow, and one day before he goes on television about civil rights. He is asking a country eight months out of the missile crisis to reconsider the enemy it had been counting warheads against.
stops.quote: In the final analysis, our most basic common link is that we all inhabit this small planet. We all breathe the same air. We all cherish our children's future.
stops.quote_source: John F. Kennedy, Commencement Address, American University, Washington D.C., 10 June 1963 (transcript, The American Presidency Project)
suggested_refs: The American University commencement address of 10 June 1963, the 'Strategy of Peace' speech

stops.name: West Berlin, Rathaus Schoneberg: Ich bin ein Berliner
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He comes to West Berlin twenty-two months after the Wall is built and stands on a platform before the Schoneberg town hall with the square and the streets behind it filled. He has looked over the Wall that morning from a viewing stand. The German sentence he has practised phonetically is delivered twice, at the opening and at the close, and the crowd noise on the recording buries the second delivery for several seconds. The day before he had spoken at the Romerberg in Frankfurt about Atlantic partnership. Nobody remembers the Frankfurt speech.
stops.quote: All free men, wherever they may live, are citizens of Berlin, and, therefore, as a free man, I take pride in the words "Ich bin ein Berliner."
stops.quote_source: John F. Kennedy, Remarks at the Rudolph Wilde Platz, Berlin, 26 June 1963 (transcript, JFK Library / ushistory.org)
suggested_refs: The Rudolph Wilde Platz before the Rathaus Schoneberg, 26 June 1963

stops.name: New Ross, the homestead at Dunganstown
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The day after Berlin he lands in Ireland and drives out to Dunganstown in County Wexford, to the farmyard his great-grandfather left for Boston, and takes tea with the cousins who stayed. The Irish press covers four days of it without pause. Nothing is negotiated on the visit. A president of the United States stands in a farmyard because his family came out of it, and that is the whole purpose of the journey. He tells them he will come back in the spring.
suggested_refs: The Kennedy homestead at Dunganstown, near New Ross, County Wexford; RTE Archives film of the visit

stops.name: Rome, the audience with Paul VI
stops.date_confidence: attested. The pool's claim that he was the first sitting US president received by a pope is false and is corrected in the campa: Wilson was received by Benedict XV in January 1919 and Eisenhower by John XXIII in December 1959.
stops.campa: On the second of July he is received in private audience by Paul VI, elected pope days before, in the opening week of that pontificate. He is not the first American president a pope has received: Woodrow Wilson was received by Benedict XV in 1919 and Eisenhower by John XXIII in 1959. He is the first Catholic one, and that is the whole difficulty. He had promised the country during the campaign that no churchman would tell him how to govern it, and in the Vatican he shakes the pope's hand rather than kissing his ring, a gesture the American papers report within the day.
suggested_refs: The audience with Paul VI, 2 July 1963, in the first week of his pontificate
sources: NPR, 'The Complicated History of Popes and U.S. Presidents'

stops.name: Hyannis Port, the death of Patrick
stops.date_confidence: birth 7 August 1963 and death 9 August 1963 attested. The pin is the compound, where the family was staying; the birth was in fact by emergency caesarean at Otis Air Force Base Hospital, Bourne, and the death at Boston Children's Hospital, for neither of which does the pool supply coordinates.
stops.campa: His wife, at the Cape for the summer, goes into labour early and is taken to the hospital at Otis Air Force Base, where a son, Patrick Bouvier Kennedy, is delivered by caesarean on the seventh of August. The lungs are unfinished. The child is moved to Boston and dies there on the ninth of hyaline membrane disease, two days old, with his father in the room. The president is photographed leaving the hospital by himself. Those who know the marriage say it changes in the three months that are left of it.
suggested_refs: Otis Air Force Base Hospital, Bourne, and Boston Children's Hospital, 7-9 August 1963

stops.name: Fort Worth, the Hotel Texas: the last morning
stops.date_confidence: corrected: the pool dated this 21 November. He arrived in Fort Worth on the night of the 21st and slept in Suite 850, but the parking-lot speech and the Chamber of Commerce breakfast both took place on the morning of 22 November, and in that order, which the pool also had reversed.
stops.campa: He has slept in Suite 850 of the Hotel Texas. On the morning of the twenty-second he comes out into a wet parking lot across the street and speaks without a coat to a crowd that has stood in the rain to wait for him, then goes back inside to address the Fort Worth Chamber of Commerce at breakfast in the Crystal Ballroom. The rain stops by mid-morning. The aircraft that will carry him the short hop to Dallas is already being readied at Carswell, for the sake of the arrival rather than the distance.
suggested_refs: National Archives Prologue, 'The Hours before Dallas'; the Crystal Ballroom breakfast, 22 November 1963
sources: National Archives Prologue, 'The Hours before Dallas'

stops.name: Love Field, the crowd at the fence
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Air Force One lands at Love Field before midday. There are crowds against the fence and the Kennedys work them for several minutes, shaking hands through the wire, before the motorcade forms up for the run downtown to the Trade Mart, where he is to speak at lunch. The car is an open Lincoln with the top off, because the weather has cleared. The route has been printed in the Dallas papers. He is in Texas at all to settle a quarrel between two wings of the state Democratic party before next year's campaign.
suggested_refs: The undelivered Trade Mart address of 22 November 1963

stops.name: Dealey Plaza, the shots
stops.date_confidence: attested. The pool's afterlife lens gives 32.7799, -96.8083 for this plaza and its geography lens 32.7799, -96.8085; the file uses -96.8085 throughout so the assassination and the museum share a pin.
stops.campa: At half past twelve the motorcade turns off Houston Street into Elm and slows through the curve beneath the Texas School Book Depository. Shots are fired from the sixth floor of that building. He is hit in the back and neck and then in the head; Governor Connally, in the seat ahead of him, is wounded. The car accelerates out of the plaza toward Parkland. The Warren Commission will find one gunman firing three shots; the House Select Committee will find, on acoustic evidence afterward disputed, probably two. The plaza itself is not altered in any way and can still be walked.
suggested_refs: The Warren Commission report (1964) and the House Select Committee on Assassinations report (1979)

stops.name: Parkland Memorial Hospital, Trauma Room One
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He is carried into Trauma Room One a few minutes after the shots. The head wound is not survivable and the doctors work on him anyway. He is pronounced dead at one o'clock, and a priest gives conditional last rites. The Dallas county medical examiner tells the party that Texas law requires the autopsy to be done here; the argument is settled by the Secret Service taking the coffin out of the building. At thirty-eight minutes past two Lyndon Johnson takes the oath aboard Air Force One at Love Field, with the widow standing beside him in the clothes she has worn since morning.
suggested_refs: Trauma Room One, Parkland Memorial Hospital; the oath aboard Air Force One at Love Field

stops.name: Bethesda, the autopsy in the night
stops.date_confidence: attested. Corrected pin: the pool gave 38.9847, -77.0961, about 1.9 km south; the National Naval Medical Center at 8901 Rockville Pike is at 39.0017, -77.0947.
stops.campa: The aircraft lands outside Washington after dark and the body goes by ambulance to the National Naval Medical Center at Bethesda, chosen by the widow because he had been a naval officer. The autopsy is performed that night. It will be criticised for the rest of the century as rushed, and its forensic detail contested in every reexamination that follows, including the House Select Committee's. The questions about the wounds start in this building, and each reexamination since has had to begin by reexamining the autopsy.
suggested_refs: The Bethesda autopsy of 22 November 1963 and its review by the House Select Committee on Assassinations
sources: Wikipedia, Walter Reed National Military Medical Center

stops.name: Havana, Castro on television
stops.date_confidence: attested. Canonical Havana pin inherited byte-identical from the Castro and Lansky files (23.1136, -82.3666).
stops.campa: In Havana, the day after Dallas, Fidel Castro goes on television to say that the death of a man, even an enemy, does not make them happy, and that a crime of this kind touches the sensitivity of any man at all. He warns his own country that the killing is likelier to strengthen the reactionary forces in Washington than to weaken them. Two and a half years earlier he directed the defence at the Bay of Pigs against a brigade this man had sent. The casinos taken from Meyer Lansky three years before are shut, and the embargo the two of them built between them will outlive both.
stops.quote: The death of a man, even though this man may be our enemy, does not make us happy.
stops.quote_source: Fidel Castro, television address on the assassination of John F. Kennedy, Havana, 23 November 1963 (transcript, kennedysandking.com)
suggested_refs: Castro's television address of 23 November 1963, transcript at kennedysandking.com

stops.name: The Capitol Rotunda, lying in state
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The flag-draped casket lies under the dome and the line to pass it runs out of the building and into the winter night; about two hundred and fifty thousand people file past in the hours the doors are open, and the doors are kept open past the announced hour for the ones still waiting. Ninety-eight years earlier the same rotunda held Abraham Lincoln's coffin. The next day the cortege walks from the White House to the Cathedral of St Matthew the Apostle behind the widow and the two brothers, and on across the river. The country watches all of it on television, which has broadcast nothing else for three days.
suggested_refs: The lying in state, 24 November 1963, and the Requiem Mass at St Matthew's, 25 November

stops.name: Arlington, the flame lit by hand
stops.date_confidence: attested. Coordinate contradiction in the pool, flagged and not adjudicated: its geography lens gives 38.8829, -77.0703 and its afterlife lens 38.8829, -77.0716, about 110 m apart; the file uses the afterlife figure, which was researched for the gravesite itself.
stops.campa: He is buried on the slope below Arlington House, on ground his widow chooses against the family's wish to take him back to Massachusetts. She asks for an eternal flame and the Army has about a day to build one: a propane tiki torch got from the Washington Gas Light Company, fed by lines the engineers run two hundred yards from a tank, lit by her hand at the graveside and then by Robert's and Edward's. In December the infant Patrick and an unnamed stillborn daughter are reinterred beside him. The improvised burner is meant to last until something permanent can be built.
suggested_refs: The improvised eternal flame of 25 November 1963, built in a day by the Army Corps of Engineers
sources: Wikipedia, John F. Kennedy Eternal Flame

stops.name: Hyannis Port, one brief shining moment
stops.date_confidence: attested: the interview took place 29 November 1963 and the Life piece ran 6 December. The pool's afterlife lens pinned it at 41.6362, -70.2856; the file uses the corrected compound coordinate for consistency with the other Hyannis Port stops.
stops.campa: One week after Dallas she summons Theodore White of Life magazine to the Cape through a storm and talks for hours. What she hands him is a frame: the record played at night before sleep, the closing lyric of a Broadway musical, one brief shining moment that was known as Camelot. White's editors think the theme overplayed. She stands over the copy and overrules them, and the piece runs on the sixth of December. He writes afterward that she was setting the myth before the bitter accounts could be written. His notes go to the library at Columbia Point sealed until a year after her death.
suggested_refs: Theodore White's Life essay of 6 December 1963 and his sealed interview notes at the JFK Library
sources: Time, 'Jackie Kennedy Movie: Read the Real LIFE Magazine Interview'
Washington Post, 'How Camelot Lived Happily Ever After'
History.com, 'Why Is JFK Associated With Camelot?'

stops.name: The White House, the Fermi Award given by another man
stops.date_confidence: attested; carried independently by two existing atlas files. Canonical White House pin inherited byte-identical from the Lincoln file.
stops.campa: He had chosen Robert Oppenheimer himself for the Enrico Fermi Award, a rehabilitation of the man whose security clearance the government stripped in 1954, and he is killed ten days before the ceremony. Lyndon Johnson hands over the medal in the East Room on the second of December, in the room and on the date Kennedy had set. Earlier that year Kennedy created the modern Presidential Medal of Freedom, superseding the Truman-era decoration that Eisenhower had given John von Neumann in 1956. The honours he scheduled are conferred on time by a man who did not choose them.
suggested_refs: The Enrico Fermi Award ceremony, East Room, 2 December 1963

stops.name: Runnymede, an acre of the meadow
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Britain gives the United States an acre of the meadow at Runnymede where Magna Carta was sealed in 1215, and Geoffrey Jellicoe lays out a memorial on it: a path of granite setts climbing through a wood to a single stone. Elizabeth II and Jacqueline Kennedy dedicate it on the fourteenth of May 1965. The gift is ceremonial and the ground stays British in law, whatever the guidebooks say about standing on American soil. The stone is inscribed with the paragraph from the inaugural address, in a field that is the origin story of the constitution he swore to.
suggested_refs: The Kennedy Memorial at Runnymede by Geoffrey Jellicoe, dedicated 14 May 1965
sources: Big Think, 'Is this acre in England really American territory?'

stops.name: Arlington, the permanent flame
stops.date_confidence: attested: casket moved March 1967, site consecrated and opened 15 March 1967, memorial complete by 20 July 1967. Same coordinate contradiction as the burial stop, flagged there.
stops.campa: After nearly two years of building, the casket is taken up before dawn in March 1967 and moved a short distance to the permanent grave; the site is consecrated and opened on the fifteenth and finished by July. The flame now burns at the centre of a five-foot circle of flat granite at the head of the grave, from a nozzle with a constantly flashing electric spark that relights the gas whenever rain or wind or a visitor's coat puts it out. It has not been out since. Jacqueline Kennedy is buried beside him in 1994. Their son is not: he is scattered at sea off Martha's Vineyard in 1999.
suggested_refs: The permanent gravesite and eternal flame, Arlington National Cemetery, opened 15 March 1967
sources: History.com, 'JFK's body moved to permanent gravesite'
JFK Library, 'President Kennedy's Grave in Arlington National Cemetery'
Britannica, 'Where is John F. Kennedy, Jr., buried?'

stops.name: Dealey Plaza, the crowd that waits for the son
stops.date_confidence: attested. Same pin as the assassination stop; the pool's afterlife lens gives -96.8083 for the museum, a difference of about 20 m, not adjudicated.
stops.campa: The Texas School Book Depository has been the Sixth Floor Museum since 1989, and the plaza below takes pilgrims all year, a good share of them walking to the grassy knoll rather than to the window. On the second of November 2021 several hundred gather there at half past twelve, the hour of the shots, on the word of a gematria practitioner that John F. Kennedy Jr., dead in a plane crash in 1999, will appear alive and be made vice president under a reinstated Donald Trump. He does not appear. The crowd moves on to a Rolling Stones concert to wait for him there instead.
suggested_refs: The Sixth Floor Museum at Dealey Plaza; Snopes on the gathering of 2 November 2021
sources: The Sixth Floor Museum at Dealey Plaza (jfk.org)
Snopes, 'QAnon Believers Went to Dealey Plaza Expecting Arrival of Deceased JFK Jr.'
